name: Every build stamps itself
idea: The version is worked out from the code by the system every time a copy is built or released, so nobody has to remember to stamp it.
tradeoff: Every build, even a throwaway one, now carries a version, so the rule that it can also be run by hand must still be offered.
recommended: Removes a manual step that can be forgotten, so no released copy can carry an empty version, while keeping the committed record empty and every rule intact.

steps.intent: Build or release a copy of the program.
steps.system: Works out the version from the code the copy is built from: the tag, commit count and short commit name when tags exist, a short commit name otherwise.

link.reason: The system derives the version as part of building instead of waiting for someone to run a separate stamping step.

steps.intent: Know which code this copy came from.
steps.system: Records that version in the copy only; the committed source keeps an empty version.

link.reason: Separating the recording from the deriving makes it clear the committed record is never changed.

name: Stamp on request
idea: Someone asks for the version to be stamped, either by hand or as part of releasing, and gets confirmation of what was recorded.
tradeoff: Still depends on someone or the release process asking, so a hand-made build can carry an empty version.

steps.intent: Stamp the program with the current version.
steps.system: Replaces the empty version with the text for the current commit, tag-based when tags exist and short commit name otherwise.

link.reason: Keeps the explicit stamp as the single place the version is written.

steps.intent: Confirm what was stamped.
steps.system: Shows the version that was recorded.

link.reason: Today nothing reports the result, so a wrong stamp goes unnoticed.

name: Install in one go
idea: The person asks for the definitions and the system picks the usual folder, installs everything and reports; choosing another folder is an option, not a required step.
tradeoff: People who want another folder take one extra, optional step before starting.
recommended: The common case needs one request and one answer, and every rule on permissions, replacement, languages, locking and failure is kept.

steps.intent: Get the current policy definitions.
steps.system: Proposes the operating system's own policy definitions folder as the destination every time and fetches the one fixed Microsoft package.

link.reason: The destination is filled in so the person only has to ask.

steps.intent: Wait while the definitions are installed.
steps.system: Locks the destination and the start, prevents leaving while it runs, takes control of an existing destination for an administrator, unpacks the package and removes it, then replaces files in the destination with the templates, the regional-format language files and the English fallback, resetting permissions.

link.reason: Unpacking, taking control and moving are one piece of work the person only waits for.

steps.intent: Learn the result and use the definitions.
steps.system: Tells which step failed if any, re-enables everything and reports no new folder; on success removes scratch files and asks whether to open them, reporting the folder only on yes.

link.reason: The outcome is clear and the person decides whether to open the folder.

steps.intent: Install somewhere other than the usual folder, only when needed.
steps.system: Replaces the destination with the folder chosen; cancelling leaves it unchanged.

link.reason: Choosing a folder is rarely needed, so it is offered only when wanted.

name: Choose, install, review
idea: The person confirms where the definitions go, the system installs them in clearly separate stages, and then the person reviews the outcome.
tradeoff: More steps and an explicit choice every time, even for the usual folder.

steps.intent: Decide where the definitions will live.
steps.system: Offers the operating system's own policy definitions folder as the starting destination every time; a chosen folder replaces it and cancelling leaves it unchanged.

link.reason: The destination is visible and confirmed before anything changes.

steps.intent: Start getting the definitions.
steps.system: Fetches the one fixed package, and from then on blocks a second start, changes to the destination and leaving.

link.reason: Starting is separate from choosing so the person commits knowingly.

steps.intent: Prepare and unpack the definitions.
steps.system: For an administrator takes control of an existing destination; unpacks the package and removes it when successful.

link.reason: Preparing the destination before moving makes failures easy to name.

steps.intent: Put the definitions in place.
steps.system: Replaces same-named files with the templates, the regional-format language files and the English fallback, and resets permissions.

link.reason: Installing is the one stage that changes the person's files, so it is shown on its own.

steps.intent: Review the outcome.
steps.system: Reports any failed step and re-enables everything, or on success clears scratch files and asks whether to open the folder, reporting it only on yes.

link.reason: The result and next action are stated plainly.

name: Offer once, keep it open
idea: On first use the system works out whether definitions are lacking and makes a single offer, and if it is passed over the invitation stays quietly available.
tradeoff: Needs a standing invitation, which is more to design than a one-time question.
recommended: The person is never lost if they decline once, the offer is still made only once, and the lack of definitions is worked out without asking.

steps.intent: Start using the program for the first time.
steps.system: Records that the offer has been considered, even if none is made, and never considers it again.

link.reason: Recording the consideration is separated so it holds whatever the outcome.

steps.intent: Have missing definitions noticed without having to check.
steps.system: Works out whether the edition lacks Group Policy support and whether more than two non-empty categories name a missing parent.

link.reason: The system decides on evidence so only people who need the offer see it.

steps.intent: Accept or put off the definitions.
steps.system: Makes the welcome offer; yes starts getting the definitions.

link.reason: The person decides whether to download.

steps.intent: Come back to the definitions later.
steps.system: Keeps a standing invitation to get the definitions available without repeating the offer.

link.reason: Today the text only says it can be done later; a standing invitation makes that real.

name: First-run question
idea: At first use, if definitions are lacking, one question asks whether to download them now.
tradeoff: A person who declines is left to find the later route themselves.

steps.intent: Open the program for the first time.
steps.system: Records that the offer has been considered and does not consider it again.

link.reason: Marks the offer as considered at once.

steps.intent: Be offered the definitions only if they are missing.
steps.system: If the edition has no Group Policy support and more than two non-empty categories name a missing parent, asks the welcome question and starts the download on yes.

link.reason: Deciding and asking happen as one moment.

name: Check, then switch
idea: The new definitions are fully checked beside the current ones, and only when they are ready do they replace the current ones in one step.
tradeoff: The system must hold two sets of definitions for a moment, and what the person sees only changes at the end.
recommended: It keeps the person's working definitions untouched until the new ones are known to be usable, and still needs no decision from the person when all goes well.

steps.intent: Say that the downloaded definitions should become the ones in use.
steps.system: The system takes the downloaded folder and finds the template files in it, ignoring everything else.

link.reason: Choosing the folder and loading it become one request instead of a window followed by a load.

steps.intent: Be sure each template comes with its text in my language.
steps.system: The system picks the language text for each template, preferring the person's language, then the same language family, then English, and refuses a template with none or with a flawed text.

link.reason: Finding the language text is its own visible stage so a missing language is named rather than left to a vague failure.

steps.intent: Be sure the templates are sound.
steps.system: The system reads and validates every template beside the current definitions, skipping and listing the ones it refuses and stopping at once on a missing namespace.

link.reason: Checking comes before replacing, so a bad download cannot spoil what the person has.

steps.intent: Understand what the policies, categories and products mean.
steps.system: The system works out the categories, products, support rules, policies, options and their layouts for entering values, with their names and descriptions in the language.

link.reason: Everything is worked out from the template once, ahead of use, rather than as the person browses.

steps.intent: Switch to the new definitions.
steps.system: The system empties the workspace, adds the staged definitions to the available ones, and remembers the folder as the definitions folder; with no new folder nothing changes.

link.reason: Emptying, loading and remembering are one switch that either happens whole or not at all.

steps.intent: Know what went wrong.
steps.system: The system shows nothing when all loaded, otherwise lists each problem, and asks whether to continue only where a choice is wanted.

link.reason: Problems stay visible and the question is asked only when it matters.

steps.intent: Start working with the new definitions.
steps.system: The system presents the category tree with nothing selected, the empty state in the information pane, and previous search results forgotten.

link.reason: The person lands on a clean, predictable view.

steps.intent: See each policy's setting and comment as before.
steps.system: The system works out each policy's state and comment in each area from the stored settings and the live ones, and applies the filters.

link.reason: The rules of states and filters stay exactly as they are, with no change for the person.

name: Hand over on arrival
idea: The moment a download is complete the system checks it, switches to it and only speaks up about problems.
tradeoff: The person gives up the moment of control over when the switch happens, which may surprise someone mid-work.

steps.intent: Get the download done.
steps.system: The system treats a finished download as the request to use it, finding the template files and the matching language text without being asked.

link.reason: The person asks for nothing beyond the download itself.

steps.intent: Trust the result.
steps.system: The system validates, reads and builds the definitions, and replaces the workspace and remembers the folder when they are usable.

link.reason: Everything that used to need a separate load is done as the default.

steps.intent: Hear only about problems.
steps.system: The system says nothing when all loaded, otherwise lists the problems and asks about continuing only where a choice is wanted.

link.reason: Silence means success.

steps.intent: Carry on from a fresh view.
steps.system: The system shows the category tree with nothing selected and the empty state, and forgets earlier search results.

link.reason: The new definitions are ready at once.

steps.intent: See each policy's setting and comment as before.
steps.system: The system works out each policy's state and comment and applies the filters.

link.reason: The rules of states and filters stay as they are.

name: Preview and confirm
idea: A single prompted path shows what the download holds and what would change, and the person confirms before the current definitions are replaced.
tradeoff: Adds a confirming step for people who just want it done.

steps.intent: Point to the downloaded definitions.
steps.system: The system finds the template files in the downloaded folder.

link.reason: The starting request is as simple as before.

steps.intent: See what the download holds.
steps.system: The system checks the templates and their language texts and tells how many categories, products and policies it holds and which templates it refuses and why.

link.reason: Seeing the content and problems first lets a rarely-used person decide with knowledge.

steps.intent: Confirm replacing what I have.
steps.system: The system, on a yes, empties the workspace, adds the definitions, remembers the folder, and on a no changes nothing.

link.reason: The replacement is asked at the point it is understood, not before.

steps.intent: Know what went wrong.
steps.system: The system lists the problems that remain and asks whether to continue only where a choice is wanted.

link.reason: Problems are still reported in full.

steps.intent: Start working with the new definitions.
steps.system: The system shows the category tree with nothing selected and forgets earlier search results.

link.reason: The person begins from a clean view.

steps.intent: See each policy's setting and comment as before.
steps.system: The system works out each policy's state and comment and applies the filters.

link.reason: The rules of states and filters stay as they are.

name: Resume where I left off
idea: Everything the person last worked with is brought back in the order they care about, and anything wrong is reported once, in one place.
tradeoff: The person waits for all sources and the definitions to be ready before the first view appears.
recommended: Keeps every rule, removes the scattered notices by reporting the state of the workspace once, and is the simplest to explain: what you left is what you get.

steps.intent: Have my preferences remembered
steps.system: Recovers the remembered preferences; when they cannot be kept, carries on with defaults and does not stop the person.

link.reason: Preferences are the base for everything that follows and keep their quiet fallback.

steps.intent: Get back to the policy sources I used last
steps.system: Reopens the remembered user and computer sources, or the local Group Policy on first start; closes any sources already open, works out each source's location and whether it can be saved, and falls back to the defaults with a notice when the remembered ones cannot be reached.

link.reason: Choosing, opening and checking the sources is one outcome, so it is one step with no questions.

steps.intent: Get the policy definitions I last used
steps.system: Loads the definitions from the remembered folder, or the system default, and offers the default when the remembered folder fails; when the problems found are minor, asks whether to keep the partly loaded set.

link.reason: Definitions decide what can be browsed, so they are loaded before anything is shown.

steps.intent: Have my policy comments alongside
steps.system: Finds the comments that belong to each source; a source whose comments cannot be read simply has none.

link.reason: Comments are separate from the sources and their failure no longer hides inside the sources step.

steps.intent: Know whether the workspace is ready to change
steps.system: States once which sources can be fully changed and which can only be viewed or kept in memory, and names the sources; says nothing beyond the notice when everything is writable.

link.reason: One summary replaces separate notices per source.

steps.intent: Browse everything
steps.system: Shows the categories with user and computer policies together.

link.reason: Starting on the broadest view means nothing is hidden at first.

name: Open now, settle in the background
idea: The person can browse the definitions at once while sources and comments are opened, checked and reported as they become ready.
tradeoff: Changing policy has to wait until the sources are confirmed, so the person may start browsing before they can edit.

steps.intent: Browse the policy definitions immediately
steps.system: Recovers preferences (continuing with defaults if they cannot be kept), loads the definitions from the remembered folder or the system default, and shows all categories of user and computer policy.

link.reason: Definitions are the one thing browsing needs, so they come first.

steps.intent: Have my sources ready without asking
steps.system: In the background, reopens the remembered sources, works out their locations and whether they can be saved, and uses the defaults with a notice if the remembered ones cannot be reached.

link.reason: The system already knows what was used last, so the person is not asked.

steps.intent: See my comments when I open a policy
steps.system: Finds comments for the sources only when a policy with comments is first needed; unreadable comment files leave that source without comments.

link.reason: Comments are not needed to browse, so reading them is put off.

steps.intent: Be told what I cannot yet change
steps.system: Shows, as soon as the sources are open, which can be fully changed and which not.

link.reason: A state that appears when it becomes known replaces a notice at start.

name: Name the language, then reload
idea: The person states the language, the system checks it is well formed and changed, saves it, and offers to apply it now.
tradeoff: The person still has to know the code of the language.
recommended: Smallest change that keeps every rule while making the apply-now choice part of the same moment.

steps.intent: Say which language the definition text should use
steps.system: Checks the language is two parts around a hyphen and refuses it with a plain message otherwise; closes without change when it equals the language already stored.

link.reason: Entry and checking are one request.

steps.intent: Have the language remembered and applied
steps.system: Saves the language at once and asks whether to reload the workspace now; if yes, clears it and reloads the definitions from the saved folder, otherwise it applies at the next load.

link.reason: The person decides when the cost of reloading is paid.

name: Pick from the languages I have
idea: The system shows the languages it finds among the installed definitions, preselects the current one, and applies the choice after confirmation.
tradeoff: A language whose files are not installed must be entered by hand, which keeps the free entry path alive.

steps.intent: Choose a language from those available
steps.system: Lists languages the installed definitions carry, marks the current one, and still accepts a typed language; refuses a typed language not made of two parts around a hyphen; picking the current one changes nothing.

link.reason: Offering the known languages saves knowing codes and prevents typos.

steps.intent: Apply it
steps.system: Saves the language, then offers to reload now or at the next load.

link.reason: Same moment for choice and result, with the person's say on reloading.

name: Leave and let go
idea: Leaving releases every source on its own and says so only when something could not be released.
tradeoff: Nothing is offered to the person when a resource is busy beyond the notice.
recommended: Matches the outcome exactly: leave, with everything released and nothing to do in the normal case.

steps.intent: Finish and leave
steps.system: Releases each open source, unloading any mounted user hive, and ends the work.

link.reason: Cleaning up and closing are one leaving, not two.

steps.intent: Know if anything was left open
steps.system: Tells the person when resources are still open in other programs.

link.reason: Silent on success, specific on failure.

name: Leave with a retry
idea: If a source cannot be released, the person is shown which and chooses to retry or leave anyway.
tradeoff: An extra decision in a rare case, and the person may be kept from leaving.

steps.intent: Ask to leave
steps.system: Releases each open source, unloading any mounted user hive, and records which succeeded.

link.reason: Same cleanup.

steps.intent: Decide what to do about anything still held
steps.system: Tells the person that resources are still open in other programs and which; lets them retry or leave anyway.

link.reason: A held source is a real decision the old notice gave no way to act on.

steps.intent: Leave
steps.system: Ends the work.

link.reason: The program ends once the person has decided.

name: Ask who and which version
idea: On request the person sees the author, the address and, when known, the version.
tradeoff: The version is only seen when asked for.
recommended: Enough for a one-fact task; nothing is added that the person did not ask for.

steps.intent: Find out who made this and which version I have
steps.system: Shows the author and the project address, and the version only when a version was built into the program.

link.reason: Already a single step.

name: Version always in sight
idea: The version is shown wherever the person is working, with the author and address a step away.
tradeoff: Takes a little room on the main view all the time.

steps.intent: See which version I am using without asking
steps.system: Shows the version beside the person's work when a version was built into the program.

link.reason: Support questions start with the version, so it need not be requested.

steps.intent: Learn more about the maker
steps.system: Shows the author and project address.

link.reason: Author details are needed rarely.

name: Say where each side lives
idea: The person states the home of the user policies and of the computer policies, giving details only for the kinds that need them, and the system opens both.
tradeoff: Both choices are made together, so a failure on one side blocks the other until it is fixed.
recommended: Closest to the outcome: decide the two homes and begin, with the system asking for nothing that the choice does not need.

steps.intent: Say where the user policies are kept
steps.system: Offers local files, the system settings store, a policy file, a particular user's policy or a user profile, or an empty scratch space; asks for the detail only for the kind chosen and accepts only policy files of the right type, including one not yet created.

link.reason: Choice and its detail are one request, shown only when relevant.

steps.intent: Say where the computer policies are kept
steps.system: Same, for the computer side, without the per-user kinds.

link.reason: Same shape as the user side.

steps.intent: Name the user whose own policy object is used, if I chose that
steps.system: Hands over to naming a user and returns that user's SID.

link.reason: A per-user policy needs a named user.

steps.intent: Confirm and start working
steps.system: Creates both sources; if either cannot be created, says which and why and stays open; otherwise opens them, shows the outcome, and moves to the nearest visible category.

link.reason: Creating and opening happen when the person confirms, with one report.

steps.intent: Change my mind
steps.system: Leaves everything as it was.

link.reason: Cancelling is always free.

name: Accept what is proposed
idea: The system proposes the remembered sources, checks they can be opened, and the person only changes a side that is wrong.
tradeoff: People who always want something different pay one extra look.

steps.intent: See the sources I would be working against
steps.system: Shows the remembered user and computer sources, or local Group Policy first time, with a note whether each can be opened and changed.

link.reason: Most visits want the same sources.

steps.intent: Change one side only if it is wrong
steps.system: For the side to change, offers the same kinds as today, asking the detail only for the kind chosen, including a policy file that does not exist yet and a named user's policy or user profile.

link.reason: Detail is asked only for the side that changes.

steps.intent: Go ahead
steps.system: Creates and opens both sources; says which failed and why when not possible, then shows the result and the nearest visible category.

link.reason: A single confirm replaces separate acceptance and opening.

steps.intent: Back out
steps.system: Leaves everything as it was.

link.reason: Cancelling is always free.

name: Give a name or an identifier
idea: One entry for either a user name or an identifier; the system works out which it is, translates a name itself and confirms the account in one go.
tradeoff: Relies on the directory being reachable to turn names into identifiers.
recommended: Collapses look-up, check and confirmation into one request while keeping every message the person can meet.

steps.intent: Say which user I mean
steps.system: Takes a name or a security identifier; a name is translated at once and the person is told when it cannot be; a valid identifier is accepted; an invalid one is refused with a message saying what to enter; leaving without choosing is always possible.

link.reason: Search, check and cancel need no separate steps.

name: Choose from known accounts
idea: The system offers the accounts it knows and the person picks one, with typing as the fallback.
tradeoff: Needs the directory to list accounts, and long lists must be searched.

steps.intent: Pick the user from the accounts available
steps.system: Offers known accounts for choosing, and also accepts a typed name or identifier.

link.reason: Choosing is easier than remembering a name.

steps.intent: Check the chosen user
steps.system: Translates a name to an identifier and tells the person when it cannot; refuses an invalid identifier with a message; stays open if no identifier results.

link.reason: Same checks as today.

steps.intent: Back out
steps.system: Leaves without choosing.

link.reason: Cancelling is always free.

name: Choose from the profiles
idea: The person sees the profiles on this computer and chooses the one whose settings are to be the user policy source, or leaves without choosing.
tradeoff: The person must still recognise their profile among several.

steps.intent: Find the profile whose settings should be the user policy source
steps.system: The system lists the profiles stored on this computer and offers none as chosen until the person selects one.

link.reason: The choice stays explicit, so nothing is picked by accident.

steps.intent: Confirm the chosen profile
steps.system: The system reports the chosen profile's settings location as the user policy source and finishes the choice.

link.reason: Choosing and confirming read as one outcome, with the settings location worked out by the system.

steps.intent: Change my mind and leave without choosing
steps.system: The system closes the choice with nothing chosen and leaves the current source as it was.

link.reason: Leaving is always possible and harmless.

name: Start from my own profile
idea: The system proposes the signed-in person's own profile and the person only confirms, or picks another.
tradeoff: A guess can be wrong when the person means another profile, so it must be easy to change.
recommended: Fewest steps for the common case, with the explicit-choice rule still enforced and cancel always available.

steps.intent: Accept or replace the proposed profile
steps.system: The system proposes the profile of the person using the program, lists the others, and does nothing until one is selected and confirmed.

link.reason: Most people edit their own profile, so the common case needs one confirmation and no searching.

steps.intent: Leave without choosing
steps.system: The system closes the choice with nothing chosen and the current source unchanged.

link.reason: Leaving is always possible and harmless.

name: Whose settings?
idea: The system asks whose settings are to be edited (my own, another person on this computer) and then narrows to that profile.
tradeoff: Adds a question for people who already know which profile they want.

steps.intent: Say whose settings to edit
steps.system: The system offers my own profile or the other profiles on this computer and waits for an answer.

link.reason: A first question in plain words helps people who do not know what a profile is.

steps.intent: Confirm the profile found
steps.system: The system names the profile and reports its settings location as the user policy source once confirmed.

link.reason: The person sees whose settings they chose before it takes effect.

steps.intent: Stop at any point
steps.system: The system closes the choice with nothing chosen.

link.reason: Leaving works at every point of the question.

name: Review, then save
idea: The person sees what will be saved and to which sources, saves, and then reads the outcome of each source.
tradeoff: One extra look before saving for people who just want to save.

steps.intent: See what will be saved and where
steps.system: The system shows each chosen source with the settings and comments pending for it.

link.reason: People cannot see today where changes will land before saving.

steps.intent: Save the comments
steps.system: The system writes each source's comments first, with generated ids and in the fixed comment format, replacing earlier content; sources without comments are skipped.

link.reason: Comments are their own stage so a problem there is visible apart from settings.

steps.intent: Save the settings to each source
steps.system: The system writes a source only if fully writable, reporting otherwise that it is not writable, storing values in the policy file encoding and updating the source in the way its kind needs.

link.reason: Each source kind is handled by one rule set, hidden from the person.

steps.intent: Have the changes take effect where possible
steps.system: The system refreshes policy for local and per-user group policy sources, applies the difference to the running account where the edition has no group policy, and notes what will apply later or was discarded.

link.reason: Taking effect is stated as its own outcome.

steps.intent: Remember the chosen sources
steps.system: The system remembers the source types and locations for the next start.

link.reason: Sources are remembered only after saving.

steps.intent: Read what happened
steps.system: The system reports success with the user and computer outcomes, or failure with the reason.

link.reason: One clear summary replaces scattered messages.

name: Save in one go
idea: The person asks once to save and the system does everything, then reports each source's outcome.
tradeoff: The person has no chance to review before the system writes.
recommended: One request does the whole job with the outcome per source told afterwards, keeping every ordering and per-source rule.

steps.intent: Save my changes
steps.system: The system saves comments, writes each fully writable source (otherwise reporting it is not writable), makes the changes take effect where possible, and remembers the chosen sources, using the same rules for every source kind and file encoding.

link.reason: One request, no sub-decisions: the system works out how each source takes effect.

steps.intent: Know the outcome of each source
steps.system: The system reports success with a line per source, such as saved, already applied, will apply later or discarded, or failure with the reason.

link.reason: The outcome per source tells the person what is live without asking.

name: Check first, then save
idea: The system first checks that every source can be written and says what will happen, then saves on the person's go-ahead.
tradeoff: Two stages even when all is well.

steps.intent: Find out whether everything can be saved
steps.system: The system checks that each source is fully writable and says per source how the change will take effect.

link.reason: Failing late, after some sources are written, is avoidable by checking first.

steps.intent: Go ahead and save
steps.system: The system saves comments first, then writes the sources that are fully writable, in the policy file encoding and the way each source kind needs, and remembers the chosen sources.

link.reason: The save happens only once the person has seen what will happen.

steps.intent: Read the result
steps.system: The system reports success with user and computer outcomes, or the reason for failure.

link.reason: The same result summary closes the task.

name: Decide and save
idea: Pick where the policy applies, decide its state, set only the options that matter, and save in one closing step.
tradeoff: Still asks the person to walk the options one by one, so a policy with many options takes a while.

steps.intent: Choose the policy's scope and see what it is
steps.system: The system shows the policy's name, help and support text, the side it applies to (computer or user, fixed when the policy has one only), whether that side can be changed, and the state it is in today.

link.reason: One step shows the policy and its scope and reloads the state when the side changes, instead of two separate moments.

steps.intent: Decide the policy's state: on, off or not configured
steps.system: Options become editable only when on is chosen; the other two states need nothing more.

link.reason: The state decision comes first so the person is asked for options only when they matter.

steps.intent: Fill in the options
steps.system: Each option shows the value stored today or its default, within its limits; numbers outside limits are brought back to the limit, text is capped, choices are sorted as the definition says.

link.reason: Options start from what is stored so the person changes only what they want to change.

steps.intent: Edit list entries where an option is a list
steps.system: The person adds, removes and names entries; the system refuses two entries with the same name and ignores the empty spare row.

link.reason: Entering and collecting list entries is one piece of work, not an editor opened and closed.

steps.intent: Add a comment on why
steps.system: Where the source keeps comments the person can record a reason; where it does not, the system says comments are unavailable.

link.reason: The reason for a change is asked for as its own small step, not hidden among options.

steps.intent: Save and either carry on or finish
steps.system: The system forgets what the policy held, writes the chosen state, options and comment, and then keeps the person on the policy or leaves it, reporting a change if anything was saved earlier.

link.reason: Saving, saving and leaving, and reporting the outcome are one decision.

drops.reason: How extra width is shared is a matter of presentation with no rule behind it; the target lays out its own space.
The old behaviour of leaving a policy half set when a chosen choice does not exist is a defect; the target writes a policy all together or not at all and refuses a choice that does not exist.

name: Review what will change
idea: The system loads the current state and every stored option, the person states what they want, and a forecast of exactly what will be written and removed is confirmed before saving.
tradeoff: Needs the system to compute and show a forecast of changes before writing, which is extra work to build.
recommended: Fewest steps, and the person sees every value that will be written or removed before it happens, which is where the old way surprised people (all options written, whole list keys cleared).

steps.intent: Open the policy with everything already worked out
steps.system: The system fills in the policy's description, applies to side, state and stored options, defaults and comment, and shows whether this side can be written to.

link.reason: Nothing is asked that the system can read for itself.

steps.intent: Say what state it should be in and change only what differs
steps.system: The person picks on, off or not configured and edits only the options that need to change; the system keeps values within limits and refuses duplicate list names.

link.reason: State, options and lists are changed in one place, with the options available only when on.

steps.intent: Review the forecast of changes
steps.system: The system lists what will be forgotten, written and removed, including whole list keys and values taken away by Disabled, and what the comment will become.

link.reason: Showing the effect before it happens is new and prevents unintended writes.

steps.intent: Confirm, then carry on or finish
steps.system: The system applies the forecast, reports the outcome as a change if anything was saved in this visit, and keeps the person on the policy or closes it.

link.reason: One confirmation covers saving and leaving.

drops.reason: How extra width is shared is a matter of presentation with no rule behind it; the target lays out its own space.
The old behaviour of leaving a policy half set when a chosen choice does not exist is a defect; the target writes a policy all together or not at all and refuses a choice that does not exist.

name: Walk me through it
idea: One prompted question at a time: where it applies, what state, each option in plain words, a reason, and a summary to confirm.
tradeoff: More steps for people who do this often, who get no shortcut.

steps.intent: Say where the policy applies
steps.system: The system asks only when the policy applies to both computer and user; otherwise the side is set and noted.

link.reason: Scope is asked first because everything after it depends on it.

steps.intent: Say what should happen to the policy
steps.system: The system explains the policy using its help and support text, shows today's state and asks whether to turn it on, off or leave it unset.

link.reason: The question is asked in plain words with the explanation beside it.

steps.intent: Answer each option, one at a time
steps.system: Only when on is chosen the system asks each option in turn with today's value or default prefilled and applies limits, lengths and sorting.

link.reason: Options are asked only after the state and one at a time, so nothing is shown that is not needed.

steps.intent: Fill in any list one entry at a time
steps.system: The system asks for each entry and, where entries are named, checks names are not repeated.

link.reason: A list is built entry by entry instead of in a grid.

steps.intent: Leave a reason
steps.system: If comments are kept for this source the system asks for a reason, otherwise it says they are unavailable.

link.reason: A guided path asks for the reason explicitly.

steps.intent: Check the summary and confirm
steps.system: The system summarises the state, options and comment, then writes them and offers to carry on or finish, reporting a change if anything was saved.

link.reason: The summary and the save are one confirmation.

drops.reason: How extra width is shared is a matter of presentation with no rule behind it; the target lays out its own space.
The old behaviour of leaving a policy half set when a chosen choice does not exist is a defect; the target writes a policy all together or not at all and refuses a choice that does not exist.

name: Check, then apply
idea: The person supplies the text, sees what it holds and any fault with its line, then confirms applying it.
tradeoff: Three steps, so a person who only wants to apply a known-good text still passes a check step.

steps.intent: Provide the semantic policy text, from a stored file or by entering it, or start again from a blank one.
steps.system: Takes the whole text as given, replacing what was there; a fresh start asks for confirmation and restores the signature line and blanks. Anything parsed earlier is discarded.

link.reason: One step for every way of getting text in, and no leftover result from an earlier try.

steps.intent: Know whether the text is good before anything changes.
steps.system: Reads the text, and states the number of policy settings found or the reason and line it failed on; nothing is applied.

link.reason: A fault is found and located before it can cost anything.

steps.intent: Apply the settings.
steps.system: Accepts only text that reads correctly, writes each policy to the computer or user source by its section, skips and counts those that fail, and reports success or how many could not be applied.

link.reason: The one step that changes anything is separate and explicit.

drops.reason: Dismissing a window and selecting text in a box are ways of using a control; backing out is still free because nothing is applied until the person says so (the discard rule is kept).

name: Bring in with live check
idea: The system reads the text as soon as it arrives, shows the count or fault at once, and offers to apply only when the text is good.
tradeoff: The person cannot apply a text the system has not already accepted, so there is no way to force a partly bad one through.
recommended: Fewest steps and a text can never be applied unchecked, while every reading, applying and failure rule stays.

steps.intent: Bring in the text, from a file or entered.
steps.system: Reads it straight away and states the count of policy settings or the line and reason of the first fault; replaces earlier text, and drops any earlier result.

link.reason: Check happens by default instead of being asked for, saving a step.

steps.intent: Apply what was read.
steps.system: Offers apply only for a text that read correctly, then writes, skips and counts failures per policy and reports the outcome.

link.reason: Apply needs no separate check step before it.

drops.reason: Dismissing a window and selecting text in a box are ways of using a control; backing out is still free because nothing is applied until the person says so (the discard rule is kept).

name: Read, then copy
idea: The person reads the settings as text, chooses whether the signature line is included, and copies it.
tradeoff: Two steps where copying is separate from reading.

steps.intent: See the chosen policy settings as semantic policy text, with or without the signature line.
steps.system: Shows the text, starting with the heading and a blank line only when the signature line is wanted.

link.reason: The choice of heading is made where the text is seen.

steps.intent: Take a copy of the whole text to use elsewhere.
steps.system: Provides the whole text for use elsewhere.

link.reason: Copying the whole text is the purpose of the task.

drops.reason: Selecting text is a control gesture; copying takes the whole text so it is not needed.

name: Ready to take away
idea: The system gives the text in the form the person will use, ready to take, with the signature line included by default so it can be imported back.
tradeoff: Assumes the common reason is to reuse the text; the heading choice is still offered but moves out of the way.
recommended: One step to the outcome, and the text is importable by default.

steps.intent: Take the policy settings as semantic policy text.
steps.system: Provides the whole text ready to use elsewhere, with the heading and blank line by default, or without when the person asks for only the fragment.

link.reason: One step reaches the purpose; reading is possible but not required.

drops.reason: Selecting text is a control gesture; copying takes the whole text so it is not needed.

name: Name it, then go
idea: The person gives an identifier, sees what kind of thing it is, then goes to it.
tradeoff: Recognition and going stay as two steps.

steps.intent: Give the identifier of a category, product, support definition or policy.
steps.system: Trims it and tries category, product, support definition then policy in that order, cutting a user or computer suffix first, and shows the kind found, nothing found, or nothing yet.

link.reason: The person sees what the identifier means before leaving.

steps.intent: Go to what was found.
steps.system: Opens a category if visible, else says it is not visible; opens a policy in the computer area in preference to user, within its visible category, and tells the person when it is hidden; shows a product or support definition with its details; says not found otherwise.

link.reason: Going is a deliberate step.

drops.reason: Where the cursor starts and how a window is dismissed are control details; nothing changes unless the person goes to the thing.
Confirming an identifier that matched nothing is replaced by telling the person it was not found; the hidden deduplicate entry could not be started and has nothing to carry.

name: Type and arrive
idea: The system recognises the identifier and takes the person there in one step, telling them plainly when it cannot.
tradeoff: A mistyped identifier that happens to match something takes the person there at once.
recommended: One step from identifier to destination, and the person is told when a policy is hidden instead of nothing happening.

steps.intent: Name what is wanted by its identifier and arrive there.
steps.system: Trims the text, resolves the kind in order and any suffix, then opens it as the outcome rules say, or says it was not found.

link.reason: Recognising and going are one action, saving a step.

steps.intent: Read the details of a product or support definition reached.
steps.system: States the kind, parent, version, children, and how a support definition matches and lists its entries.

link.reason: Details are shown only for what has them, not as a dialog every time.

drops.reason: Where the cursor starts and how a window is dismissed are control details; nothing changes unless the person goes to the thing.
Confirming an identifier that matched nothing is replaced by telling the person it was not found; the hidden deduplicate entry could not be started and has nothing to carry.

name: Ask, then search
idea: The person says which words and where to look, then sees the policies that match.
tradeoff: Choosing where to look is always offered, even for the common all-three search.

steps.intent: State the words or phrases remembered and where to look: title, description or comments.
steps.system: Requires some words and at least one place to look, with all three chosen by default; understands plain words, wildcards and quoted phrases.

link.reason: Words and places are stated together.

steps.intent: See the policies that match.
steps.system: Lists a policy when any chosen place, including comments from both areas, contains every word, wildcard and phrase.

link.reason: Results are a clear outcome step.

drops.reason: Dismissing a window is a control detail; a search that is not started changes nothing.

name: Search as you type
idea: The system looks in all three places as the words are given, and narrowing the places is an option.
tradeoff: Searching on every change does more work and may show results for half-typed words.
recommended: The usual search is one step and the person learns about an unclosed quote instead of silently getting wider results.

steps.intent: Say the words or phrases remembered.
steps.system: Searches title, description and comments of both areas by default, and shows results as words are given; says plainly when words are needed and when a quote was never closed.

link.reason: No separate action to start, and the common case needs no settings.

steps.intent: Narrow where the words are looked for, if wanted.
steps.system: Limits the search to the chosen places and never allows none.

link.reason: Asked only when the person wants to narrow.

drops.reason: Dismissing a window is a control detail; a search that is not started changes nothing.

name: Describe the setting
idea: The person states the key, the value, or both, is told at once if the terms cannot be used, and gets the matching policies.
tradeoff: Still asks the person to know whether the text they have is a key or a value name.

steps.intent: Say which system setting is wanted, by its key, its value name, or both.
steps.system: Takes what was entered as the start of a search.

link.reason: Naming the setting is the one thing the task needs; nothing else is asked.

steps.intent: Learn straight away whether the terms can be used.
steps.system: Refuses an empty search and a key that begins with a root key, saying what to change, before any search starts.

link.reason: Checking before the search starts spares the person a wait that ends in a refusal.

steps.intent: Get the policies that control the setting.
steps.system: Matches key paths and value names without regard to case, with wildcards, prefixes and path parts as stated, and keeps a policy when one of its settings meets every term.

link.reason: The matching rules stay exactly as the business defines them.

steps.intent: Change their mind before searching.
steps.system: Leaves everything as it was and starts no search.

link.reason: A person can always back out of describing a search.

name: One line, split for me
idea: The person pastes or types whatever they have in one line, such as a full setting path ending in a value name, and the system works out which part is the key and which the value, checking as they go.
tradeoff: The system may guess the split wrongly for ambiguous text, so it must show how it read the text.
recommended: Fewest steps and least to know: one entry, the system infers the split and shows how it read it, while every matching and refusal rule is kept.

steps.intent: Give whatever is known about the setting in one go, such as a path copied from documentation, a key, or a value name.
steps.system: Works out which part is the key and which the value, and shows the reading so it can be corrected.

link.reason: Removes the need to know in advance which box a piece of text belongs to.

steps.intent: See at once whether the terms can be used.
steps.system: While the person types, says that nothing has been entered or that a root key must be removed, and does not search until the terms are usable.

link.reason: Feedback comes while typing, not after pressing search.

steps.intent: Get the policies that control the setting.
steps.system: Shows policies as soon as the terms are usable: a policy matches when one setting it reads or writes meets every term, ignoring case, with wildcard, prefix, whole-name and path-part rules for keys and values.

link.reason: The search runs from the entry itself, with no separate request step.

drops.reason: There is no separate request to cancel; clearing the entry abandons the search.

name: Guided lookup
idea: For people who rarely search by setting, a short prompted path asks what they know, explains the forms a key or value may take, and then searches.
tradeoff: More steps than the other variants, so slower for people who search often.

steps.intent: Say what is known about the setting: its key, its value name, or both.
steps.system: Explains with examples how keys (a part, a path start, a wildcard pattern) and value names (whole name, wildcards) are read.

link.reason: A rare user is told how terms are read before entering them.

steps.intent: Enter the key and the value.
steps.system: Takes them as the start of a search, refusing an empty pair and a key starting with a root key, and says what to change.

link.reason: Refusals state the fix in the business's words.

steps.intent: Review how the terms will be read, then confirm.
steps.system: Restates the search in plain words before it runs.

link.reason: A rare user wants to confirm the reading before waiting for results.

steps.intent: Get the policies that control the setting.
steps.system: Matches as the business defines, one setting meeting every term, ignoring case.

link.reason: Matching stays as defined.

steps.intent: Back out at any point.
steps.system: Closes the prompted path with no search run.

link.reason: Leaving is always possible.

name: Results as they arrive
idea: Hits appear for the person to work with while the search is still running, so they can open one early, stop when they have enough, and come back to the same results later.
tradeoff: Results change under the person's hands while the search runs, so the list must keep the person's place.
recommended: Removes the wait for a finished search: the person starts reviewing at the first hit, and returning to earlier results is automatic.

steps.intent: Watch the policies that match appear as the search goes.
steps.system: Clears earlier results, starts with a start message, tests every policy in turn, adds each hit with its category in policy order and keeps progress current as it goes.

link.reason: Review can begin at the first hit instead of after the whole search.

steps.intent: Stop the search once enough has been found, or leave it.
steps.system: Cancels the search; leaving before it ends marks it as cancelled with progress full.

link.reason: One way to end a search covers both stopping and leaving.

steps.intent: Know how the search ended.
steps.system: Reports checked policies and hits, or that the search was cancelled, and no longer offers stopping.

link.reason: The outcome is always stated.

steps.intent: Pick the policy to open from the hits.
steps.system: Accepts only a chosen hit, remembers its position, opens that policy's editor in the current area and moves the policy list to it.

link.reason: Picking is the point of the task.

steps.intent: Move on to the next hit.
steps.system: Takes the next hit still shown after the last one chosen, says there are no more when none is left, and returns nothing when no search ran.

link.reason: Stepping through hits is how a list is worked.

steps.intent: Come back to the last results later.
steps.system: Shows the previous results without a new search and selects the earlier choice if still present; tells the person when no search has been run.

link.reason: Returning to results needs no separate mode.

drops.reason: Pure presentation of a list (column width, drawing); they carry no business rule and the target's own list handles them.

name: Worklist beside the policy
idea: Hits become a worklist that stays with the person while they read each policy, so stepping to the next hit never means going back to the list.
tradeoff: Needs room to keep the worklist and a policy in view together.

steps.intent: Run the search and wait for its outcome.
steps.system: Clears earlier results, tests every policy in turn, adds each hit with its category in policy order, shows progress as it goes and reports the outcome.

link.reason: The search itself stays the same.

steps.intent: Cancel a search not worth finishing.
steps.system: Cancels the search and says it was cancelled.

link.reason: Stopping and leaving share one outcome.

steps.intent: Open a hit and read the policy.
steps.system: Accepts only a chosen hit, opens its editor in the current area, moves the policy list to it and keeps the worklist in place.

link.reason: The list stays visible while the policy is read.

steps.intent: Go straight to the next hit from the policy being read.
steps.system: Takes the next shown hit after the last chosen one, or tells the person there are no more.

link.reason: Next is offered where the person is reading.

steps.intent: Return to the worklist at any time.
steps.system: Shows the previous results with no new search, selects the earlier choice if present, or says no search has been run.

link.reason: Returning is one action.

drops.reason: Pure presentation of a list (column width, drawing); they carry no business rule and the target's own list handles them.

name: One hit at a time
idea: After the search the system presents hits one by one with their category, and the person opens it or moves on, for people who review without scanning a list.
tradeoff: Slow when there are many hits, and hides how many there are at a glance.

steps.intent: Search and see the first hit as soon as it is found.
steps.system: Clears earlier results, tests every policy in turn, adds hits with category in policy order and shows progress and outcome.

link.reason: Presents the first hit without a list.

steps.intent: Decide whether to keep searching.
steps.system: Cancels the search when asked, leaving it marked cancelled.

link.reason: Stopping and leaving are one choice.

steps.intent: Open this hit or move to the next.
steps.system: Opening accepts the hit, remembers its position, opens its editor and moves the policy list to it; moving on takes the next shown hit or says there are no more.

link.reason: One decision per hit.

steps.intent: Pick up where they left off.
steps.system: Reopens the last results without a search, at the earlier choice if still there, or says nothing has been run.

link.reason: The place is remembered.

drops.reason: Pure presentation of a list (column width, drawing); they carry no business rule and the target's own list handles them.

name: Live filter
idea: Choices narrow the policy list the moment they are made, with no confirm step, and a person can revert or switch the limit off at any time.
tradeoff: Every change refilters the list, so rapid changes may feel busy on a large list.
recommended: Cuts the open, choose, confirm cycle to choosing: results show the effect of each option immediately and the person can undo it.

steps.intent: See the limit currently in force.
steps.system: Shows type, state, comment and products as the current limit holds, with Any and no products when it has no such condition and the support option off with both matching options on when it has no support condition.

link.reason: The person starts from what is in force, not a blank form.

steps.intent: Choose a policy type, state and comment status.
steps.system: Keeps only managed for Policy, only unmanaged for Preference, the chosen state, and commented or uncommented as chosen; Any sets no condition. The list narrows now.

link.reason: No confirming step; each choice applies as made.

steps.intent: Limit by supported products.
steps.system: Opens product choice only while a support limit is wanted; choosing a product by hand also chooses the products under it, but loading a limit does not spread; records chosen products and both matching options, and accepts a support limit with no product.

link.reason: Product choice appears only when asked for.

steps.intent: Be taken to the right place when the limit changes.
steps.system: Turns the limit on and moves to the nearest category still shown.

link.reason: Changing a limit already means wanting it on.

steps.intent: Switch the limit on or off without losing it.
steps.system: Applies or lifts the limit and moves to the nearest category still shown.

link.reason: Switching is quick and non-destructive.

steps.intent: Start again from nothing.
steps.system: Returns type, state and comment to Any, support off, both matching options on and no product.

link.reason: A clean slate in one action.

steps.intent: Undo this round of changes.
steps.system: Puts back the limit held when the person began and leaves it unchanged.

link.reason: Backing out stays possible although choices applied live.

drops.reason: Recolouring a disabled tree is pure presentation and carries no business rule.
A double-click quirk of a tree control; the target's product choice keeps what is shown and what is kept the same by design.

name: Set up, then apply
idea: The person sets the whole limit as a draft, sees what is in force, and applies or discards it as one decision.
tradeoff: Keeps the open, choose, confirm cycle, so no fewer steps than today.

steps.intent: Begin a new limit from the one in force.
steps.system: Shows type, state, comment and products as the limit holds, or the neutral defaults when it has none.

link.reason: Starting from what is in force avoids retyping.

steps.intent: Choose type, state and comment.
steps.system: Holds the choices as a draft; Any means no condition.

link.reason: Choosing is separated from applying.

steps.intent: Choose the products, if the limit is by support.
steps.system: Available only with a support limit; a product by hand carries to products beneath it; the draft takes chosen products and both matching options, and accepts none chosen.

link.reason: Products stay optional.

steps.intent: Apply the limit, or discard it.
steps.system: Applying turns the limit on with managed, unmanaged, state, comment and support conditions as chosen and moves to the nearest shown category; discarding leaves the limit unchanged.

link.reason: One clear decision.

steps.intent: Switch the limit on or off, or reset the draft.
steps.system: Applies or lifts the limit, moving to the nearest shown category; reset returns every choice to its default.

link.reason: Both stay available.

drops.reason: Recolouring a disabled tree is pure presentation and carries no business rule.
A double-click quirk of a tree control; the target's product choice keeps what is shown and what is kept the same by design.

name: Ask what I want to see
idea: The system asks short plain questions, such as what kind, what state and whether commented, and only asks about products if the person says products matter.
tradeoff: A fixed order of questions is slower for people who know the one option they want.

steps.intent: Say what kind of policies, in what state, and with or without comments, answering only what matters.
steps.system: Shows each question with the answer in force; Any when no condition, otherwise the condition held.

link.reason: Plain questions replace a form.

steps.intent: Say whether supported products matter.
steps.system: If not, applies no support condition; if so, opens product choice, with both matching options on and no product when none is set yet.

link.reason: Products are asked only when relevant.

steps.intent: Pick the products.
steps.system: A product chosen by hand carries to those beneath it; opening from a held limit does not spread; a support limit with no product is accepted.

link.reason: Group choices are quick.

steps.intent: Confirm, with a plain summary of the limit.
steps.system: Applies the type, state, comment and support conditions, turns the limit on and moves to the nearest shown category.

link.reason: The summary prevents surprises.

steps.intent: Leave without changing anything.
steps.system: Leaves the limit unchanged.

link.reason: Leaving is safe.

steps.intent: Switch the limit on or off, or start again.
steps.system: Applies or lifts the limit and moves to the nearest shown category; reset returns every answer to default.

link.reason: Both stay.

drops.reason: Recolouring a disabled tree is pure presentation and carries no business rule.
A double-click quirk of a tree control; the target's product choice keeps what is shown and what is kept the same by design.

name: Straight to the file
idea: The person says which policy file they want to edit, sees the warning once, works in the file, and leaves when done.
tradeoff: It still asks the person to pick the area when both are file-backed, and the warning is a hard stop for first-time users.

steps.intent: Choose which policy file to edit directly
steps.system: Offers only the areas backed by a policy file, each only when the caller allows it; tells the person plainly when none is, and goes on only once an area is chosen; leaving the choice changes nothing.

link.reason: Choosing the area is the first thing the person must settle.

steps.intent: Accept, the first time, that direct editing is for advanced users
steps.system: Shows the caution; a yes is remembered so it is not asked again, a no leaves the editor closed and asks again next time.

link.reason: The warning guards a risky action and must stay.

steps.intent: See the keys and values of the file
steps.system: Lists keys alphabetically ignoring case, with sub-keys and values beneath, special deletion entries named as such, and ordinary values with their content.

link.reason: The tree is the working view of the file.

steps.intent: Know what can be done with the item in front of me
steps.system: Allows only the actions that fit what is selected: a key, a value, a deletion entry or nothing.

link.reason: Unavailable actions are never offered as choices.

steps.intent: Finish editing
steps.system: Leaves the editor; every change already made stays on the loaded policy source and reaches disk only when policies are saved, whether the person finished or backed out.

link.reason: Finishing and backing out do the same thing, so one way out is enough.

name: The system picks the area
idea: The system chooses the area when only one is backed by a policy file, shows the warning only to those who have not accepted it, and tells the person what has changed before they leave.
tradeoff: Inferring the area hides the choice from a person who wanted the other area, and the review step is new.
recommended: Takes the one question out of the usual case, folds the warning into starting, and gives a risky tool a clear account of what was changed, while every rule stays.

steps.intent: Start editing the policy file, understanding the risk the first time
steps.system: Takes the one allowed area backed by a policy file, asking only when both are and saying plainly when none is; shows the caution only to a person who has not accepted it, remembering a yes and asking again after a no.

link.reason: The choice of area and the warning become one start, with the common case needing no question.

steps.intent: Find and work on entries in the file
steps.system: Shows the file as an ordered tree, and offers only the actions that fit the selected key, value or deletion entry.

link.reason: Showing the tree and the fitting actions together keeps the person from hunting.

steps.intent: See what I have changed before leaving, then finish
steps.system: Summarises the changes made in this session and reminds the person that they reach disk only when policies are saved; leaving, however it is done, keeps the changes.

link.reason: One way out instead of two that behave the same, with an account of what was changed that the old editor never gave.

name: Guided
idea: A short prompted path for people who edit policy files rarely: accept the risk, choose the file, learn the vocabulary, then leave.
tradeoff: More steps than the others, which a regular user would find slow.

steps.intent: Accept the risk before anything else
steps.system: Explains what direct editing of a policy file does and asks for acceptance the first time; a yes is remembered, a no asks next time.

link.reason: Warning comes before choosing, so nobody does work they may then decline.

steps.intent: Choose which policy file
steps.system: Offers only the allowed areas that are backed by a policy file, tells the person when none is.

link.reason: Same choice, now after the warning.

steps.intent: Learn how to read the file
steps.system: Explains in plain words what keys, values and deletion entries are and how they are shown.

link.reason: A person who rarely edits these files needs the vocabulary before the list makes sense.

steps.intent: Browse and pick an item
steps.system: Shows the ordered tree with contents, and offers only the actions that fit the selection.

link.reason: Same tree, with the fitting actions.

steps.intent: Finish editing
steps.system: Leaves; changes already made stay on the loaded policy source until policies are saved.

link.reason: Both ways out behave the same.

name: Name, then kind, then data
idea: Adding a key is one name; adding a value is a name, a kind, then its data, each asked in turn.
tradeoff: Several small questions for a value, and a name error appears only after confirming.

steps.intent: Give the new key a name
steps.system: Asks for a name, ready to type; an empty name or backing out adds nothing.

link.reason: Naming is all a key needs.

steps.intent: Have the key created in the right place
steps.system: Refuses a name with a backslash or one already used under the same parent, ignoring case; otherwise adds the empty key under the selected key, or at the top, and selects it.

link.reason: The refusals keep the file consistent.

steps.intent: Name the new value and choose its kind
steps.system: Offers string, expandable string, list of strings, 32-bit and 64-bit number, starting on string; backing out adds nothing.

link.reason: The kind decides what data can be entered.

steps.intent: Enter the value's data
steps.system: Starts from empty text, zero or an empty list by kind; numbers stay within the limits of their size; the value is stored under the selected key only on confirming, replacing a value of the same name without warning.

link.reason: Data entry belongs with the value.

name: Checked as you type
idea: The system checks a key name while it is typed, and a value is added in one pass with its kind worked out from the data.
tradeoff: Working out the kind may guess wrongly, so the person must be able to see and override it.
recommended: Cuts the value flow from three questions to one and shows errors early, with every rule still applied.

steps.intent: Give the new key a name and know at once whether it is usable
steps.system: Checks as the person types, refusing a backslash or a name already used under the same parent ignoring case; an empty name or backing out adds nothing.

link.reason: The person learns of a problem before confirming rather than after.

steps.intent: Have the key created and selected
steps.system: Adds the empty key under the selected key or at the top and selects it.

link.reason: Same outcome as today.

steps.intent: Add a value by its name and data together
steps.system: Takes name and data in one pass; the kind starts as string and is suggested from the data (digits suggest a 32-bit number, several lines a list), stays visible and can be changed; the starting data is empty text, zero or an empty list; stored only on confirming, replacing a same-named value without warning.

link.reason: Three questions become one, and the kind is no longer asked before there is data.

name: Ask what to add
idea: One prompted path that first asks whether to add a key or a value, then asks one question at a time.
tradeoff: Slowest for someone who already knows what they want.

steps.intent: Say whether to add a key or a value
steps.system: Asks which is wanted and where, defaulting to under the selected key.

link.reason: The old editor splits this into different commands; a rare user may not know which one applies.

steps.intent: Name the key
steps.system: Asks for a name; refuses a backslash or a taken name ignoring case; empty or backing out adds nothing; the key is added and selected.

link.reason: Same naming with the refusals explained in words.

steps.intent: Name the value and choose what kind of data it holds
steps.system: Describes each kind in plain words; starts on string; backing out adds nothing.

link.reason: Explanation helps a person who does not know the kinds.

steps.intent: Enter the data
steps.system: Starts from the default for the kind, keeps numbers within their limits, and stores on confirming, replacing a same-named value without warning.

link.reason: Same entry, after the kind is understood.

name: Edit in place by kind
idea: The person selects a value, enters new data in the form that fits its kind, and chooses decimal or hexadecimal for numbers.
tradeoff: The decimal or hexadecimal choice is still a separate decision.

steps.intent: Pick the value to change and see its current data
steps.system: Shows the selected value with its present data.

link.reason: The change starts from what is there.

steps.intent: Enter the new data
steps.system: Offers text, number or list entry to match the kind; backing out leaves the value as it was.

link.reason: Entry follows the kind.

steps.intent: Choose how to read a number
steps.system: Shows and accepts numbers in decimal or hexadecimal as chosen; a hexadecimal too large becomes the largest allowed value, text that is not hexadecimal leaves the value unchanged.

link.reason: Hexadecimal is how policy authors often think of numbers.

steps.intent: Keep the change
steps.system: Replaces the data, keeps name and kind, and leaves the value selected.

link.reason: Same outcome as today.

name: Either form accepted
idea: The system accepts a number in decimal or hexadecimal as typed and shows both forms, so there is no mode to switch.
tradeoff: Guessing the form from the text can be ambiguous for digits-only input, so a clear prefix is required for hexadecimal.
recommended: Removes the mode switch while keeping every rule about size and unreadable input.

steps.intent: Pick the value and type its new data
steps.system: Shows current data, in both decimal and hexadecimal for numbers; text and lists are entered as such; backing out leaves it as it was.

link.reason: One entry replaces a mode switch and the dialog that follows it.

steps.intent: Let the system read the number, then keep the change
steps.system: Reads hexadecimal when marked as such and decimal otherwise; a hexadecimal too large becomes the largest allowed value; text that is not a number leaves the value unchanged; otherwise replaces the data, keeping name and kind and leaving the value selected.

link.reason: The person no longer has to know which mode is on, and reading and saving become one step.

name: Preview then confirm
idea: The person is shown what the value will become, with its kind and limits explained, and confirms.
tradeoff: An extra confirmation for a small change.

steps.intent: Pick the value and learn what it can hold
steps.system: Shows the kind, the present data and the limits for that kind.

link.reason: A rare user sees the limits before typing.

steps.intent: Enter the new data
steps.system: Offers entry to match the kind, in decimal or hexadecimal for numbers; a hexadecimal too large becomes the largest allowed; non-hexadecimal text leaves the value unchanged; backing out changes nothing.

link.reason: Same entry.

steps.intent: Review the result and confirm
steps.system: Shows old and new data side by side; on confirming replaces the data, keeps name and kind, leaves the value selected.

link.reason: The result is shown before it is applied so a mistyped number is caught.

name: Decide the outcome first
idea: The person first says whether the machine should be told to remove it or the file should simply forget it, then answers what that needs.
tradeoff: Two decisions are still asked of the person.

steps.intent: Choose between instructing the machine and forgetting
steps.system: Asks whether to leave a deletion instruction or remove it from this file with no trace; backing out changes nothing.

link.reason: The real choice is made first, not hidden in a dialog.

steps.intent: Say how a key is to be instructed
steps.system: For a key offers clear everything, clear then keep existing ordinary direct values, or delete one value; nothing is chosen at first, and confirming with none does nothing.

link.reason: Three real outcomes remain.

steps.intent: Name the value to delete
steps.system: The name can be entered only when delete-one is chosen; an empty name is refused; otherwise the value, whether or not it exists, is replaced by a deletion entry.

link.reason: Only relevant inputs are open.

steps.intent: Forget an entry entirely
steps.system: Asks for confirmation to remove a key with its sub-keys, values and clearing marks, or a value with its deletion entry, leaving nothing behind; no changes nothing.

link.reason: Irreversible removal stays confirmed.

name: Straight from the selection
idea: What is selected tells the system what to do: a value is marked for deletion straight away with its name known, and a key offers its choices.
tradeoff: The default for a value assumes the person wants a deletion instruction, so forgetting needs a second route.
recommended: Makes the common case, marking a value, a single act, while keeping the confirmation on irreversible removal.

steps.intent: Mark the selected value for deletion
steps.system: Takes the value's name from the selection and replaces the value with a deletion entry named "**del." and the name.

link.reason: No dialog and no typing for the most common removal.

steps.intent: Choose what to do with a selected key
steps.system: Offers clear everything, clear then keep existing ordinary direct values, or delete one value by typed name; nothing is chosen at first, none chosen does nothing, an empty name is refused, and backing out changes nothing.

link.reason: The three outcomes for a key are genuinely different.

steps.intent: Forget an entry entirely
steps.system: Describes what will go and asks for confirmation; removes the key, sub-keys, values and clearing marks, or the value and its deletion entry, with nothing left behind.

link.reason: Irreversible removal stays confirmed.

name: Ask about the machine
idea: A plain question about what should happen on the machine leads to the right removal.
tradeoff: More steps than the others.

steps.intent: Say what should happen on the computers
steps.system: Asks whether the setting should be taken away from machines that apply this file or just no longer be set by it; backing out changes nothing.

link.reason: Frames the choice in business consequences.

steps.intent: Tell the system how far to go
steps.system: For a key offers the three clearing choices described in plain words, none chosen at first; for a value takes its name from the selection or by typed name, refusing an empty one; a deletion entry replaces the value.

link.reason: Choices shown with their effects.

steps.intent: Confirm forgetting
steps.system: If it should simply no longer be set, asks for confirmation and removes the key with all its contents, or the value and its deletion entry, leaving nothing behind.

link.reason: Same confirmation.

name: Prefix worked out for you
idea: The person gives the exported settings and where they go; the system validates, works out the key prefix and reports what it found before applying.
tradeoff: Relies on the guess being right for the first key, so the person must still read the prefix the system proposes.
recommended: Fewest decisions: the prefix, which people rarely know, is asked only when the system cannot work it out, and what was found is reported before anything is applied.

steps.intent: Choose the exported machine settings and the policy source (user or computer) they should be brought into.
steps.system: The system accepts only exported-settings files and remembers the chosen source.

link.reason: File and destination are given together instead of in separate steps.

steps.intent: Be told what the file contains and how its keys will be named in the source.
steps.system: The system checks the file is a genuine export, ignores blank and comment lines, reads keys, removals, deletions and default values, works out the key prefix from the first key, and warns when the file holds default values or the prefix could not be worked out.

link.reason: The system derives the prefix and the warnings instead of making the person type or discover them.

steps.intent: Give a prefix only if the system could not decide one.
steps.system: The system refuses to continue without a file or a prefix and says which is missing.

link.reason: The prefix is asked only in the rare case it is unknown.

steps.intent: Bring the settings into the source.
steps.system: The system removes marked keys, deletes marked values, saves the others with the prefix removed from names, tells the person only that the import failed if it does, then refreshes what the person sees.

link.reason: Applying and refreshing are one outcome rather than separate actions.

steps.intent: Leave without importing.
steps.system: The system changes nothing.

link.reason: Backing out stays available at every point.

name: Guided import
idea: A short prompted path: pick the file, review what was found, confirm the prefix, then apply.
